analysis.one_liner: Cuts the estate and gift tax rate to 30% and exempts the first $10 million of an estate.
analysis.headline: A single-sponsor bill to cut estate and gift taxes for very large estates was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 2000, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2001 with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the estate and gift tax so that estates up to $10 million paid no tax at all, and anything above that was taxed at a flat 30% instead of the existing rates, which reached 55% on the largest estates. The $10 million exemption would also rise with inflation. The bill went nowhere: it was referred to the tax-writing committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, and was never taken up before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates. Under the bill, a married couple with careful planning could shield far more than $10 million from tax, and no estate below $10 million would owe anything. The wealthiest families — the ones who currently pay the 55% top rate on large fortunes — would save the most.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the graduated estate tax, which taxed the largest estates at rates up to 55%, with a flat 30% rate on everything above the exemption [S2][S3].

Raises the exemption — the amount an estate can pass on tax-free through the unified credit — from the low hundreds of thousands to $10 million, and adjusts it upward for inflation after 2001 [S2][S3].
Conforms the gift tax to the same 30% rate, so large lifetime gifts would also be taxed less [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate tax is paid only by a small number of the very largest estates, so the revenue it raises would come out of the general treasury, meaning either higher taxes elsewhere, more borrowing, or less spending on public services.

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate tax entirely on estates up to $10 million — a threshold far above what ordinary households ever reach — so the entire benefit flows to the wealthiest families while the revenue disappears from the general budget [S3].

Cutting the top rate from 55% to 30% on taxable amounts above the exemption would slash collections from the largest estates specifically, the part of the tax base that touches the fewest people and the most concentrated wealth.

Because it was a single-sponsor bill with no cosponsors and no committee action, there was never a public hearing or cost estimate on the table, so the revenue trade-off was never debated on the merits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrowly distributed: large estates pay 30% instead of up to 55%, and estates under $10 million pay nothing. The cost is broad — lost federal revenue that must be made up elsewhere — and falls on people who would never owe estate tax themselves. The design is not subtle: it is a straight transfer of tax burden from the largest inheritances to the general taxpayer.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, and sat there without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. James Leach introduced the bill on July 27, 2000 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which never acted on it [S5].
No member ever cosponsored the bill [S4].
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died in committee with no vote ever taken [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal revenue is unchanged and the tax burden on very large estates stays where it was. The narrow exception is estate-planning professionals, whose business continues intact.

for.name: Rep. James A. Leach
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; no other member joined him.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: The House committee that controls all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill's only sponsor was a Republican with zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan lineup is visible in the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: Estates above $10 million would pay 30% instead of rates up to 55%, and estates below $10 million would pay nothing. The gain comes out of federal revenue that funds services everyone uses.

industries.industry: Estate planning, trusts, and wealth management
industries.note: A higher exemption and a lower flat rate reduce the need for complex estate planning that exists mainly to manage the tax. Their interest here runs against wealthy clients' desire to pay less, but the bill died, so their business is unaffected.
